值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入探討現代社會「毛孩家人化」趨勢，以及失去寵物時常面臨的「剝奪性悲傷」與社會不理解。
  • 解析台韓等國爆紅的線上寵物紀念網站，如何扮演虛擬心靈避風港，並分析其在療癒與引發「強迫性悲傷」間的心理機制。
  • 反思最新 AI 寵物復生科技所帶來的倫理與心理依賴爭議，探討科技撫慰與接受現實之間的界線。

摘要

線上寵物紀念平台的崛起與熱潮

作者指出，近年來虛擬寵物悼念平台在社群網絡上引發廣大迴響。由紐西蘭工程師為紀念已故愛犬創立的「L」網站，上線不久便吸引近百個國家、超過兩萬隻寵物進駐，其中台灣飼主建立的紀念頁面更佔了四成，點亮逾四十萬盞虛擬蠟燭；南韓的「StarCook」平台亦在十天內湧入三十二萬人次，甚至進一步結合流浪動物認養與協尋功能。這些宛如線上寵物靈骨塔的空間，讓飼主能透過點燭、獻花、寫信與虛擬互動，傾訴對離世毛孩的無盡思念。

毛孩家人化與難以言說的「剝奪性悲傷」

現代人與寵物的羈絆日益深厚，以台灣為例，犬貓數量已正式超越十四歲以下兒童人口。研究顯示，有超過兩成的受訪者認為失去寵物的痛楚甚至超越失去人類親友，許多人更出現長期的寵物失落症候群。然而，這種巨大的悲慟在現實中常被旁人輕描淡寫地忽視，形成心理學上所謂的「剝奪性悲傷」。因為缺乏社會的同理與認可，飼主往往感到孤立且羞於啟齒，這也是線上紀念社群成為他們安全釋放情感、尋求同理關鍵場所的原因。

社群療癒效益與潛在的「強迫性悲傷」

研究表明，線上哀悼社群能為飼主提供情感宣洩與相互支持的管道，實踐心理學所倡導的「持續性連結」，意即健康的面對悲傷不需完全遺忘，而是學會在缺席中建立新的心靈連結。然而，研究同時警告群體悼念可能伴隨「強迫性悲傷」的風險，讓參與者誤以為必須時刻保持痛苦才能證明對毛孩的愛。因此，專家建議健全的紀念空間應適度引導使用者在追思與回歸日常生活中找到健康平衡。

AI 科技重塑哀悼歷程的慰藉與反思

隨著人工智慧日新月異，AI 寵物紀念技術已能重現逝去毛孩的動態影像，甚至模擬其聲音與飼主對話或寫信。儘管這項技術為悲痛的飼主帶來即時的溫暖慰藉，但專家與學術界也示警其潛在的心理與倫理風險。過度逼真的互動恐讓飼主產生心理依賴、深陷科技幻象，進而難以接受毛孩已經離開的事實。部分開發者因而主動設立機制，鼓勵使用者適時從平台「畢業」，引領人們重新思考科技究竟是幫助療癒心靈，還是阻礙了哀悼歷程的自然前行。

================================================

Do you have a pet? A website called "L" has recently gone viral on Threads in Taiwan. Just by uploading a photo of your furry friend, you can build them a dedicated memorial space in a virtual world. It became an instant hit upon launch, with thousands of pet memorial pages from Taiwan created in under two weeks; many grieving owners say it makes them cry uncontrollably. A similar site launched in South Korea and attracted over 300,000 visitors in just 10 days. More and more people now treat pets as family, and the pain of losing a pet is often just as intense as losing a human relative. In recent years, online pet memorial platforms have proliferated, and with AI becoming so advanced, even deceased pets can interact with their owners, but can these sites really help owners heal? Or do they just make it impossible to move on? Hello everyone, I’m Fan Chi-fei , welcome to Fan Chi-fei’s Special.

Report. Let’s take a look at what "L" is actually doing. Simply put, this website is like an online columbarium for pets. Users can control a small virtual avatar to wander around the site, reserve a spot for their pet who has crossed the Rainbow Bridge, or click on other pets ' photos to read the messages left by their owners. Anyone can light a candle or leave flowers for a pet they don't know, share words of comfort, or send small gifts like a can of food, a birthday cake, or. a toy; the site even features diary and sky lantern functions. The site sparked a massive trend immediately after its launch. The founder, MCH, an engineer based in New Zealand, says he originally wanted to create a 3D memorial for his dog, Bella , who passed away in 2020 at the age of 18. He mentioned that after Bella passed , no one in the family dared to speak her name because the pain was just too great. Later, he shared Bella's story online,.

and strangers left comments saying these stories helped them cope with their own loss, but he eventually worried that his memories were fading, so he decided to write them down—which inspired him to create this site to encourage others to express their grief. Since the site went live on November 1st , the founder promoted it in various languages on Threads, and it quickly went viral. According to platform statistics, as of now, nearly 100. countries and over 21,000 pets reside here. Among them, more than 8,400 pets are from Taiwan, accounting for 40%. Friends in Taiwan have lit over 400,000 candles on the platform, the highest number globally. A website that recently went viral in South Korea is called StarCook. That’s the site. According to Yonhap News, the platform launched on October 30th and accumulated approximately 320,000 visits in just 10 days. Initially, there were only 500 virtual memorial cabinets, which later.

expanded to nearly 22,000. The developer is an office worker in his 30s. He also lost two beloved cats and wanted to create a place to preserve memories, never expecting it to resonate so deeply . Beyond basic features like posting photos, writing letters, and lighting candles, this website even lets your virtual avatar walk and interact with your furry friend. Most notably, the platform recently began collaborating with animal welfare groups to establish a dedicated area for people to meet stray animals waiting for homes. There is also space for pet-finding notices,. allowing this space—originally meant for emotional comfort—to help animals in the real world that need care. In recent years, similar services have sprung up like mushrooms. Taiwan also launched "Nian-Nian Memorial " this year and "Eternal Dream Planet" in October; both focus on companionship , so you don't have to be alone. This. There are several directions to discuss regarding the popularity of such online pet memorial sites. First, the.

humanization of pets. The relationship between modern people and pets is very different from before. A 2023 survey by the Pew Research Center found that 97%of pet owners consider their pets part of the family, and 51% consider them as important as other human family members. Official surveys released in South Korea also show that about 30%of households own pets. What about here in Taiwan? As mentioned previously in "Small Inventions, Big Revolutions," one in every four households in Taiwan owns a pet. According to 2025 official statistics,. the total number of pet dogs and cats in Taiwan has exceeded 3.2 million, surpassing the number of children under 14. In other words, there are more pets than children. Second, the grief of losing a furry friend may be far more severe than we imagine. A study published in an international journal this January surveyed nearly 1,000 British adults. It found that among respondents who had experienced the deaths of both pets and human loved ones , 21%felt the loss of their pet was more devastating and painful. Many even met.

the criteria for prolonged grief disorder, meaning their sorrow lasted a long time and severely impacted their daily lives. Korean society is also increasingly recognizing "pet loss syndrome," where pet owners experience intense grief and a sense of profound loss after the passing of their beloved companion. In psychology, there is a term called "disenfranchised grief," which occurs when a person's sorrow is not understood or validated by society— something that frequently happens to pet owners. Losing a furry companion is painful enough, but those who don't understand might say, "It’s just a dog,. you can always get another one!" If anyone said that to me, I’d fight them. Even taking time off work can be dismissed as making a mountain out of a molehill. A 2021 analysis found that bereaved pet owners often feel isolated and are even embarrassed to express their grief. Other studies interviewing animal caregivers have also discovered that when grief goes unrecognized, the individuals involved are more likely to fall into isolation. So, the significance of online pet memorial sites may not just be to commemorate our furry friends, but to finally provide these "parents" a place where they can.

grieve safely, without fear of being mocked. Third, do online memorial spaces actually have a healing effect? Just this April, researchers in South Korea published a study on this topic. After interviewing 18 users of online pet bereavement communities, they found that respondents felt these groups helped them express their sadness, receive understanding, and find mutual support from others with similar experiences. However, the study also identified an unexpected issue called "compulsory grief." This means that when a group spends. every day reminiscing about departed pets, it can make some participants feel they must remain sad to prove they still love them. The researchers therefore suggest that effective online memorial sites should help users find a balance between mourning their pets and re-engaging with daily life. In psychology, there is a concept called "continuing bonds." Healthy grieving doesn't require us to completely forget the deceased, but rather to learn how to maintain a new type of emotional relationship in their.

absence. So, occasionally lighting a candle or looking at photos of a late cat or dog doesn't mean you haven't moved on; the point is to observe whether doing so helps you. It’s a step forward. Fourth, technology has made the grieving process more complex. Now, AI can not only recreate the likeness of a pet that has passed away but can even simulate interactions with their owners. For example, a Japanese owner took an old photo of their Shiba Inu from 44 years ago and. used AI to make the dog move again. In the video, the Shiba Inu not only turns its head but also tilts it toward the camera, as if it had truly returned to its owner's side. AI also provides a " letter from your pet" feature. In China , DEPS uses the pet's information and the owner's current feelings to simulate the pet's voice and write new letters, allowing owners to even write back and continue communicating. You know perfectly well that it wasn't really written by a dog, but as you read those details that only the two of you knew, you can't help but shed a tear, right?

Is this truly a form of comfort, or just an illusion manufactured by technology? A Japanese company launched the PETMemoryAI service, where owners can upload photos and personality traits of deceased pets to generate videos of them , or even chat with their owners in the pet's own "voice." However, this company is also worried about owners becoming too dependent on AI. They designed the system to avoid frequent notifications and even encourages users to eventually "graduate" from the platform, meaning to say goodbye to their virtual pet. Since. the boom in AI technology, haven't some people already started using AI to bring back deceased loved ones? This has always been a major controversy. Research from the University of Cambridge warns that this type of AI, which mimics individuals, could pose serious psychological and ethical risks . Looking back at pets, when AI allows us to constantly reunite with our deceased furry friends, is it really healing our grief, or is it making us more reliant on AI for solace, making it even harder to accept the fact that they are gone? Today, we invite everyone to chat—do you have pets? Have you used or.

would you want to try services like these? Our writer said they want to upload a photo of their "scumbag" ex-boyfriend—after all, past-tense actions should be treated as such. 值得閱讀的理由

  • 深入了解西班牙領先全球將更年期病假納入社會安全給付體系的最新政策變革與津貼制度。
  • 探討更年期症狀在歷史文化與現代職場中被「隱形化」的成因，以及高達八成受訪女性工作表現受衝擊的現狀。
  • 比較西班牙的「專項法定假別」與英國的「職場彈性環境調整」等不同應對思維，並借鏡台灣法規進行深度反思。

摘要

從經痛到更年期：女性在職場中難以言說的生理困境

作者以個人擔任駐外記者時必須仰賴強效止痛藥忍受經痛的經歷切入，描述女性步入四、五十歲後，面臨盜汗、失眠、焦慮與腦霧等更年期症狀的折磨。根據歐洲議會研究，約有85%的女性曾出現更年期症狀，更有高達三成屬於會直接影響日常工作的中重度症狀。然而，在以男性視角為主的歷史與醫學發展中，女性停經長期與喪失青春甚至負面標籤連結，導致處於事業成熟期的高階資深女性，往往在職場中對更年期身心轉變保持沉默，進而承受巨大的心理與工作壓力。

西班牙制度革新：正式將更年期嚴重症狀納入病假保障

為正視此一女性生理健康問題，西班牙政府頒布皇家法令，自2023年12月起將更年期病假正式寫入社會安全保障制度。只要經由醫師專業評估，確認症狀已暫時影響工作能力即可開立證明。該制度突破了傳統一般病假的限制，不僅取消了過去五年內須繳納180天社保的門檻，津貼更從請假第二天即開始發放，第2至20天給付60%投保薪資，第21天起增至75%，顯示政府正式肯定更年期造成的實質失能狀態。

法規專項保障與職場彈性調適的兩難抉擇

然而專項假別亦面臨落實挑戰，作者指出西班牙過去推行生理假時，許多女性因害怕被貼上「體弱多病」的標籤而不敢請假，更年期假亦恐引發雇主在招聘與晉升時的職場污名化風險。相較於西班牙的法定專假模式，英國則側重於職場環境調適，鼓勵企業提供彈性工時、改善通風與居家辦公等措施；而台灣雖有無需證明即可請取的生理假，卻未涵蓋停經後的症狀。作者認為相較於訂立難以一體適用的專項病假，推動普遍性的友善彈性工時機制，更能兼顧多元生理需求與工作效率。

I have to take painkillers, and they have to be the really strong ones prescribed by a doctor, otherwise I can't focus on work at all. Since I'm a foreign correspondent and have no one to cover for me, I can't take menstrual leave, so I always just pop pills and keep working . Around age 45 or 50, my periods started becoming irregular, and my body entered the transition period before menopause. I think I have every menopause symptom in the book: hot flashes, night sweats, insomnia, anxiety. —and what’s most infuriating is that I’ve even gotten dumber. The only comfort is that, well, everyone else goes through it too. According to data compiled by the European Parliamentary Research Service this year, about 85%of women experience at least one menopause-related symptom, with about 25 %to 30%having moderate to severe symptoms that can directly impact their daily life and ability to work. But wait —if you can take menstrual leave when period pain makes it impossible to work.

, shouldn't you also be able to take " menopause leave" when insomnia, hot flashes, and brain fog get so bad that you can't do your job? You can. But you have to live in Spain. Hello everyone, I’m Fan-chi, and welcome to Fan-chi’s View of the World from Taipei. Spain has recently decided to formally write this into their social security system. On October 20th of this year, the Spanish government passed a new royal decree. Starting December 1st. , if a woman’s menopause-related health issues are severe enough to temporarily prevent her from working, a doctor can issue a medical leave certificate. However, you don't get time off just by entering menopause. Applicants must first undergo a medical assessment. A physician must confirm the presence of menopause-related symptoms or conditions that are severe enough to affect work capacity to be eligible. The biggest difference between this and regular sick leave is the social security payment schedule.

Regular sick leave usually only receives social security benefits starting from the fourth day, but the new menopause leave is calculated from the second day . From day two to day 20, you receive 60 %of your insured salary, and from day 21 onwards, it increases to 75%. The threshold required for regular sick leave—having paid social security for at least 180 days in the past five years— has also been removed. Seen in this light, Spain isn't just giving women another type of leave; they are formally acknowledging that menopause can. sometimes be so severe that it truly makes it impossible to work for a while . Since almost every woman goes through menopause, why has it only recently started to be formally included in workplace policy discussions? One reason may be that menopause has long been associated with getting old. Research from Lancaster University in the UK has noted that the image of older women in European history is actually quite complex. Since early times, once a woman lost her fertility, it was often linked to the.

By the 18th and 19th centuries, although medicine slowly advanced, the medical system was male-dominated, so the history and treatment of menopause were primarily recorded from their perspective, with women's voices rarely preserved, leading to menopause being treated as a female condition in need of. management. This. Perhaps this also explains why, even now, many people are still reluctant to openly say at work, "My work performance has been poor lately because I'm going through menopause." Furthermore, menopause usually occurs between the ages of 45 and 55. At this age, many women are not ready to retire ; they have accumulated 20 or 30 years of work experience, may be leading teams in management roles, and are often the most experienced people in the company.

The UK government's 2024-2025 labor survey found that among those who have experienced or are experiencing menopause, as many as 82%stated that these symptoms affected their work performance to some degree, 61%found it harder to concentrate, 53%felt more stressed, and 47%felt less confident in their work abilities as a result. Therefore, menopause remains relatively invisible in the workplace, likely not because it affects few people, but. because we have long been unaccustomed to treating it as a topic for open discussion. Spain did not just suddenly think to include menopause in workplace regulations. As early as 2023, Spain became the first European country to include menstrual leave under special medical leave protections, but it is not available just because of a period; it can only be requested for conditions like endometriosis or pelvic inflammatory disease that cause pain so severe it makes working impossible. After the policy was implemented, there.

was no surge in people taking leave. Within the first 11 months of the regulation, only 1,559 instances of menstrual leave were recorded across Spain, averaging fewer than five people per day. Reasons include strict eligibility criteria requiring a doctor's diagnosis, as well as concerns among women that revealing the true reason to their company might lead to being labeled as "constantly sick." So, menopause leave is currently facing the same dilemma. On one hand, some feel that if symptoms truly affect work, the system should be adjusted. On the other, there is concern that by legally singling out women's physical needs, companies might perceive women as being more troublesome. Scholars researching labor and gender policies have noted that while such policies acknowledge the real physiological needs of women, they could also lead to stigmatization, potentially impacting employers 'decisions during hiring or promotions.
